newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - Diamonds are forever, but is De Beers?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Diamonds are forever, but is De Beers?.

text.p: In a world of free market competition, De Beers is an anachronism.
Since 1930 the South African mining giant has controlled the global diamond industry with an iron grip, operating the world's most effective cartel.
Critics say the days of its Central Selling Organisation (CSO) are numbered, but reports of its death have so far proved exaggerated.

After arguably the most difficult year in its history, De Beers thumbed its nose at the sceptics this week, reporting another sparkling set of results with year earnings up by more than a third to $1.34 billion in 1996.

The edges of the empire might be fraying -- Australia has quit the cartel and new Canadian mines may not join -- but the company's shares are riding at record highs and analysts expect sales to hit a new peak in 1997.

The London-based CSO still controls some 75 percent of all trade in uncut diamonds, selling stones worth more than $4.5 billion a year via so-called "sights" to a select group of traders and maintaining huge diamond stockpiles.
De Beers also appears to have outsmarted Moscow in a crucial poker game over Russian rough diamond sales which has unnerved the world diamond market.
RUSSIAN ROULETTE
After a stand-off late last year, Russia appears to have decided it needs De Beers' marketing skills and funding.

A stalled gem export deal between Russia, which accounts for some 20 percent of CSO sales, and De Beers is reportedly under presidential review, suggesting agreement is very close. De Beers gave few details this week but said there had been constructive talks aimed at resuming a contractual relationship.

The result could be a better deal for De Beers which has complained that Russia has been "leaking" large sought-after diamonds onto the market outside the CSO, leaving the cartel with the low-margin small stones.
If De Beers pulls it off, a viable Russian deal could be an important antidote to the loss last June of Australia' Argyle, the world's largest diamond mine, from the CSO.
That sent a shock wave through the market, although the financial impact was limited since Argyle produces mainly small stones which made up only six percent of CSO sales.
Des Mayers of stockbroker G O'Flaherty & Co even sees a silver lining in Argyle's defection, arguing that the cartel could be evolving into a "leaner and meaner" operation.
"The CSO can focus its efforts on that segment of the market it controls and where it reaps most of its profits," he said.
STRENGTH ON HOME FRONT
Nearer home De Beers' 50-50 partnership with the government of Botswana, the world's largest gem-quality producer, is as solid as ever with plans afoot to lift production by a third by 2000.

Angola may also be coming right after years of commercial anarchy. De Beers recently signed a deal to build a diamond sorting centre in Luanda, and it is talking to the government and former rebels UNITA on how to develop the mines.
Nonetheless, the doubts about the CSO's survival into the 21st century continue to nag investors and the diamond trade, especially given the emergence of powerful new competitors.

The frozen wastes of Canada could prove the key test as Anglo-Australian firm RTZ-CRA and Australia's Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd, both sceptical about the CSO, start up diamond mines with huge potential.
Any serious threat to the CSO's control of the market would not only savage the De Beers share price but shake public confidence in diamonds as a store of value.
That mutual interest in market stability is the key reason for the continued existence of the cartel, according to De Beers -- which prefers to call the CSO a producers' cooperative.
CONSUMERS KEEP FAITH
Consumers, in turn, continue to believe in the scraps of compacted carbon which maintain their price only because of their controlled rarity.
CSO rough diamond sales rose seven percent last year to a record $4.8 billion, despite Argyle's withdrawal from the cartel in June, and Mayers confidently predicts sales above $5 billion in 1997.
At the retail level the values are multiplied tenfold with global diamond jewellery sales in 1996 estimated at around $53 billion, some five percent up on 1995.
De Beers deputy chairman Nicholas Oppenheimer, grandson of Sir Ernest Oppenheimer who founded the CSO two-thirds of a century ago, is confident the tried and tested system can continue to work.
"There is a bit of life in the old dinosaur yet," he said.
